This comparison cannot be made validly on a single common basis. The firms report different quantities with no shared metric or definition: Bank of America cites use-case counts and a virtual assistant (Erica, over 58 million interactions per month; more than 300 AI/ML use cases approved and 114 live generative AI use cases); Schwab cites use-case counts, developer-productivity percentages, and client-facing positioning (40 then more than 220 use cases, ~25% developer productivity increase, and claims it is already an AI-enabled company and #1 in the space); Raymond James cites dollar technology spend (approximately $1 billion to $1.1 billion), Raimond user counts (6,500 unique users, 99.5% satisfaction), and an AI framework; Morgan Stanley cites use cases (DevGen AI, Parable, LeadIQ) and a CEO statement calling AI absolutely the top priority for the firm and existentially important, having been overweighted and now double overweight to AI in wealth; and Edward Jones cites third-party partnerships (Aboon, Quicken). Because these are different definitions, units, scopes and periods (use-case counts, dollar spend, productivity percentages, subjective positioning statements), the firms are not comparable on a like-for-like basis, so no single firm can be ranked as making the most extensive or strongest claims from this evidence alone.
